title: The Coin in the Garden
teaser: Hamdy was planting tomatoes when his shovel hit something metal.
paragraphs: Hamdy is a farmer in a village near Luxor. One morning, he is digging in his garden to plant tomatoes. His shovel hits something hard. He bends down and finds a small, dirty, round piece of metal.

He cleans it with water. It is a coin, very old, with a face of a man and strange letters around it. His son, Khaled, takes a photo and searches online. “Baba, this could be Roman,” he says. “Maybe two thousand years old!”

Some neighbours come to look. One man says, “You can sell it for a lot of money!” Hamdy thinks about it. The family needs money. But he also knows that old objects belong to the history of the country.

The next day, Hamdy and Khaled take the coin to the antiquities office in Luxor. An archaeologist looks at it with a magnifying glass. She is very excited. “This coin helps us understand trade in this area,” she explains. “There may be more objects in your village.”

A few months later, a team of archaeologists comes to the village. Hamdy helps them, and they pay him for his work. In the museum in Luxor, there is now a small card next to the coin. It says: “Found by Hamdy Abdelrahman, farmer.”

title: The Great Library of Alexandria
teaser: It tried to collect every book in the world. What really happened to it?
paragraphs: More than two thousand years ago, Alexandria was one of the most important cities in the world. Its rulers, the Ptolemies, wanted it to be a centre of knowledge, so in the third century BC they founded a great library and a research institution called the Mouseion.

The library’s goal was ambitious: to collect every book in the world. Books at that time were scrolls, long rolls of papyrus. According to ancient writers, ships arriving in the port were searched for scrolls, which were copied for the library. The scholars there studied mathematics, astronomy, medicine and literature, and some made discoveries still taught today.

Many people believe the library was destroyed in one huge fire. The truth seems more complicated. A fire during Julius Caesar’s war in Alexandria in 48 BC probably damaged part of the collection, but the library seems to have continued afterwards. Over the following centuries, political conflicts, reduced funding and the slow decay of papyrus all contributed to its decline.
In other words, the library may have died slowly, through neglect rather than a single disaster. Historians still debate the details, because few reliable sources survive.

In 2002, Egypt opened the Bibliotheca Alexandrina, a modern library near the ancient site, as a tribute to the original. Its round design, facing the sea, is meant to look like a sun rising, a symbol of knowledge returning to the city.

targets.en: to start an organisation or institution
wanting to achieve something big
a person who studies a subject deeply
a fight or serious disagreement

questions.q: What opened in 2002?

recap: The Ptolemies’ Library of Alexandria collected scrolls and scholars; it likely declined slowly through conflict and neglect; a modern library honours it.

title: The Turtle Night
teaser: Nadia filmed sea turtles for a year. The best moment happened at 2 a.m.
paragraphs: Nadia is a young filmmaker from Hurghada. She wants to make a documentary about sea turtles on the Red Sea coast. Every year, female turtles come to the same beaches at night to lay their eggs in the sand.

For a year, Nadia works with a team of volunteers. They walk on the beach every night and count the nests. They put small fences around the nests to protect them from people and dogs. They never use bright lights, because light confuses the turtles.
Filming is very hard. Nadia waits for many nights and sees nothing. Some nights, it is windy and cold. Once, a turtle comes, but Nadia’s camera battery is dead. She almost gives up.

Then, one night in August, at two in the morning, a volunteer whispers, “Look!” Dozens of tiny baby turtles are coming out of the sand. They walk quickly towards the sea, following the light of the moon on the water. Nadia films everything quietly, with a special red light.

Her documentary is shown at a film festival in Cairo. At the end, the audience stands and claps. But Nadia’s favourite moment is different: after the film, a group of children asks her how they can become volunteers.

title: How Nature Documentaries Capture the Impossible
teaser: A few minutes of a snow leopard can take three years to film.
paragraphs: When you watch a nature documentary, you see a cheetah running at full speed, a whale feeding in the deep ocean or a rare leopard on a mountain. What you do not see is the enormous effort behind each shot. A single sequence of a few minutes can take months or even years to film.

Patience is the main tool. Camera teams often wait in small hides, camouflaged shelters, for weeks, hoping an animal will appear. They study animal behaviour with scientists first, so they know where and when to wait.

Technology helps a lot. Camera traps, triggered by movement or heat, film shy animals while nobody is there. Drones film herds from above without disturbing them. Special cameras can shoot thousands of frames per second, turning a hummingbird’s wings or a falling drop of water into beautiful slow motion.

Sound is often added later. It is almost impossible to record clear sound from far away, so many sounds you hear, like footsteps in snow or the crunch of a leaf, are recreated in a studio. Some critics say this blurs the line between reality and storytelling.

Modern documentaries also show the human impact on nature: plastic in the oceans, melting ice and disappearing forests. Many filmmakers hope that if people fall in love with the natural world on screen, they will want to protect it in real life.

recap: Nature documentaries rely on patience, hides, camera traps, drones and slow motion; sounds are often recreated; filmmakers hope to inspire protection.

title: The Mystery of the Missing Cake
teaser: A birthday cake disappeared from the fridge. Detective Lamia is on the case.
paragraphs: It is Grandma’s seventieth birthday. Mum made a big chocolate cake and put it in the fridge at three o’clock. At six o’clock, when the guests arrive, the cake is gone. The plate is empty and clean.

Lamia is twelve and loves mystery stories. “I will find the thief,” she announces. She takes a notebook and a pen. There are four suspects: her brother Ziad, her cousin Malek, Uncle Fathy and the cat, Mishmish.

First, she looks for clues. There are chocolate marks on the kitchen door. They are high, so it was not the cat. Ziad was at football practice all afternoon, and his coach confirms it. Malek is allergic to chocolate; he cannot eat it.

That leaves Uncle Fathy. When Lamia asks him where he was, he says, “Sleeping on the sofa.” But Lamia notices something: there is a small brown mark on his white shirt. “Uncle,” she says, “why is there chocolate on your shirt?”

Uncle Fathy’s face turns red. Then he laughs and confesses. He did not eat the cake. He hid it, because he ordered a surprise second cake and wanted Grandma to have the bigger celebration. He takes everyone to the balcony, where both cakes are waiting. Grandma laughs so much she cries.

a person who steals

title: Why Your Fingerprints Are Unique
teaser: Even identical twins have different fingerprints. Here is why.
paragraphs: Look closely at your fingertips and you will see tiny ridges forming loops, arches and spirals. These patterns help you grip objects, but they are also famous for another reason: no two people, as far as we know, have exactly the same fingerprints. Not even identical twins.

Fingerprints form before birth, around the tenth week of pregnancy. Their general shape is influenced by genes, but the fine details depend on tiny random factors: the position of the baby in the womb, the pressure of the fluid around it and the speed at which the skin grows. Because these conditions are never exactly the same, the final pattern is unique.

Experts compare fingerprints by looking for minutiae, small details such as a ridge that ends suddenly or splits into two. A typical print contains many of these points, and their positions create a pattern that can be compared with records in a database.

Fingerprints were first used systematically to identify criminals in the late nineteenth century, and a police office in Argentina solved one of the first cases with them in 1892. Today, computers can compare a print with millions of others in seconds.

However, fingerprint analysis is not perfect. Partial or smudged prints can lead to mistakes, and there have been cases of people wrongly accused. Modern investigators usually combine fingerprints with other evidence, such as DNA and cameras, before reaching a conclusion.

recap: Fingerprints form before birth with random details, making them unique; experts compare minutiae, but mistakes happen, so other evidence is used too.

title: The Fourth Floor
teaser: Every night at midnight, someone knocked on the empty flat’s door.
paragraphs: Karim and his family move to a new building in Alexandria. Their flat is on the third floor. The flat above them, on the fourth floor, is empty. The doorman says nobody has lived there for ten years.
On the first night, at exactly midnight, Karim hears a sound from upstairs. Knock. Knock. Knock. Three slow knocks. Then silence. The next night, the same thing happens. And the next.

Karim cannot sleep. He tells his sister, Yasmine. She laughs at first, but on the fourth night, she hears it too. Her face goes white. “Let’s go and look,” she whispers. Karim does not want to go, but he does not want to look scared.

At midnight, they climb the dark stairs with a torch. The knocking starts again. It is coming from inside the empty flat. Karim’s hand is shaking. Yasmine pushes the door. It is not locked. It opens slowly with a long creak.

Inside, they see dust, old furniture… and a window that is open. On the window, a loose wooden shutter moves in the sea wind and hits the wall. Knock. Knock. Knock. Yasmine starts laughing. Karim closes the shutter. They go down the stairs very fast anyway.

targets.en: a man who works at the entrance of a building
to hit a door to make a sound
a small electric light you carry

options: A loose shutter in the wind

options: A small electric light you carry

recap: Karim and Yasmine hear knocks from an empty flat at midnight; brave enough to look, they find a loose shutter banging in the wind.

title: Why Do People Enjoy Being Scared?
teaser: Your heart races, you scream — and you buy another ticket.
paragraphs: Fear is supposed to protect us. When we sense danger, the body releases adrenaline, the heart beats faster, breathing quickens and muscles prepare to fight or run away. So why do millions of people choose to watch horror films, ride frightening roller coasters or visit haunted houses?

The key is safety. Researchers who study recreational fear say we enjoy it most when the threat feels real enough to excite us, but we know deep down that we are safe. The body experiences the rush of fear, while the mind knows the monster is only on a screen. When the scary moment ends, many people feel relief and even a kind of high.

There seems to be a sweet spot. If the experience is too mild, it is boring; if it is too intense, it stops being fun and becomes truly unpleasant. People differ in where that point is, which explains why one friend loves horror and another refuses to watch.

Fear can also be social. Watching a scary film together creates shared reactions: screaming, grabbing someone’s arm, laughing afterwards. Some studies suggest that these moments can bring people closer.

Interestingly, some psychologists think horror stories also help us practise. By imagining dangerous situations safely, we rehearse how we might react. During difficult real-world events, some horror fans even reported feeling slightly better prepared.

targets.en: to feel or notice something

a good feeling when something bad ends

options: We feel the rush but know we are safe

recap: We enjoy fear when the body feels the rush but the mind knows we are safe; there is a sweet spot, it bonds people, and it may help us rehearse danger.

title: The Ramadan Table
teaser: Every evening, Abdallah set up a table on the street. One guest changed everything.
paragraphs: Abdallah owns a small grocery shop in Shubra. Every Ramadan, he puts a long table outside his shop at sunset. It is a mawa’ed el-rahman, a free iftar table. Anyone can sit and break their fast: workers, students, delivery drivers and travellers.

His wife and daughters cook all afternoon: rice, beans, chicken, salad and dates. His son, Yehia, helps him carry the plates and the big bottles of water. It is hard work, but the street feels like one big family.

One evening, a young man sits at the end of the table. He is quiet and does not eat much. Abdallah notices that he comes every day, always alone. After a week, Abdallah sits next to him. “Where are you from, my son?”

The young man’s name is Bilal. He came from Aswan to Cairo for work, but the job ended and he has very little money. He is ashamed to tell his family. Abdallah listens. The next day, he asks Bilal to help in the shop for a salary.
Years later, Bilal has his own shop in Aswan. Every Ramadan, he puts a long table outside it. When people thank him, he says, “Don’t thank me. Thank a man in Shubra who asked me one question.”

title: Why Ramadan Moves Every Year
teaser: The Hijri calendar follows the moon, not the sun. Here is how it works.
paragraphs: If you remember Ramadan in the summer heat as a child and now it comes in cooler months, you have noticed something important about the Islamic calendar: it moves through the seasons. This happens because the Hijri calendar is lunar, based on the moon, while the calendar used for everyday life, the Gregorian calendar, is solar, based on the sun.

A lunar month is the time between one new moon and the next, about 29.5 days. So Hijri months have either 29 or 30 days, and a Hijri year of twelve months has about 354 days. A solar year has about 365 days. The difference is around eleven days, which means that Ramadan begins about eleven days earlier each year in the Gregorian calendar.
Over roughly 33 years, Ramadan passes through every season. A person who lives a long life will fast Ramadan in winter, spring, summer and autumn several times.

Traditionally, a new month begins when the thin crescent of the new moon is seen after sunset. Because sighting depends on location and weather, different countries sometimes start Ramadan or celebrate Eid on different days. Today, many also use astronomical calculations to predict the start of each month.

The calendar counts years from the Hijra, the migration of the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, from Mecca to Medina in 622 CE. That is why years in this calendar are marked with AH, from the Latin phrase meaning “in the year of the Hijra”.

title: The Worry Box
teaser: Hana worried about everything, all the time. Her counsellor gave her a box.
paragraphs: Hana is a first-year student at Ain Shams University. She is clever, but she worries all the time. She worries about exams, about her friends, about her future and about things she said three years ago. At night, her thoughts go round and round, and she cannot sleep.

Her friend tells her about the university counsellor. Hana is nervous, but she goes. The counsellor, Dr. Mona, is calm and kind. She listens for a long time. Then she gives Hana a small wooden box and some paper.

“When a worry comes,” Dr. Mona says, “write it on a paper and put it in the box. Then tell yourself: I will think about this at six o’clock.” Every day, at six o’clock, Hana opens the box and reads her worries for fifteen minutes. After that, she closes it.

It sounds strange, but it helps. During the day, Hana can focus more. At six o’clock, many worries do not seem important anymore. Some of them already have solutions. Some of them she cannot control, and she learns to let them go.

Hana still worries sometimes. Everyone does. But now her worries have a place and a time, and they do not control her whole day. She keeps the box on her desk, and next to it, a note from Dr. Mona: “A thought is not a fact.”

title: Nobody Is Watching You as Much as You Think
teaser: The spotlight effect, and why it should make you braver.
paragraphs: Imagine you walk into a lecture hall and trip on the step. Your face burns, and for the rest of the day you think everyone saw it and is talking about it. Psychologists have a name for this feeling: the spotlight effect. We tend to believe that other people notice our appearance and our mistakes much more than they really do.

In a well-known experiment in the United States, students were asked to wear an embarrassing T-shirt into a room full of other students. Afterwards, the wearers estimated that about half of the people in the room had noticed the shirt. In reality, only around a quarter had.

Why does this happen? Each of us is at the centre of our own experience. We know every detail of our hair, our accent and our clumsy moment, so we assume these details are equally obvious to others. But other people are busy with their own spotlight: their own appearance, their own worries.

The spotlight effect has a cousin called the illusion of transparency: the belief that our nervousness is clearly visible. Speakers often think the audience can see how anxious they are, but listeners usually notice much less.

Understanding this can be freeing, especially for language learners. That grammar mistake you made yesterday? The other person probably forgot it within seconds. Knowing that others are not watching that closely can give you the courage to speak, ask questions and try new things.

title: Grandpa’s Boat
teaser: Every plank has been changed. Is it still the same boat?
paragraphs: Seif’s grandfather is a fisherman in Rashid. He has a small wooden boat called Al-Amal, which means hope. He bought it fifty years ago, and he still goes fishing in it every morning.
One day, Seif helps his grandfather paint the boat. Seif asks, “Grandpa, is this the same boat you bought fifty years ago?” Grandpa laughs. “Of course! It is Al-Amal.”

But then Grandpa starts to think. Over the years, he changed the old wooden planks one by one, when they became weak. He changed the motor three times. He changed the seats and the ropes. “Actually,” he says slowly, “I think there is not one piece of the old boat left.”

Seif is confused. “So it is not the same boat?” Grandpa scratches his head. “It has the same name, the same shape and the same captain. Every morning it takes me to the same sea. Is a thing its pieces, or is it its story?”

They sit on the beach and think about it for a long time. Seif says, “Our body changes too. Are we the same person we were as babies?” Grandpa smiles. “Now you are a philosopher,” he says. “Pass me the paint.”

title: The Trolley Problem: Would You Pull the Lever?
teaser: A runaway train, five people, one lever. There is no easy answer.
paragraphs: Imagine a runaway trolley, a kind of tram, speeding down a track. Ahead, five workers are on the line and cannot escape. You are standing next to a lever. If you pull it, the trolley will switch to a side track, where it will hit one worker instead of five. Do you pull the lever?

Most people say yes: saving five lives at the cost of one seems better. This answer reflects a way of thinking called consequentialism, which judges an action by its results. The best choice is the one that produces the most good, or the least harm.

Now change the story. There is no lever. You are on a bridge above the track, next to a very large man. If you push him onto the track, his body will stop the trolley and save the five. The numbers are the same, yet most people refuse to push. Why?

Many philosophers say this shows the influence of another approach, often linked to the German philosopher Immanuel Kant. It argues that some actions are wrong in themselves, whatever the results, such as using a person merely as a tool. Pulling a lever feels like redirecting harm; pushing someone feels like killing him.

The trolley problem is not really about trains. It appears in debates about self-driving cars, medical decisions and war. It shows that our moral intuitions are complex, and that reasonable people can disagree about what is right.
